overview.text: Alfred Hitchcock’s 1960 black-and-white film Psycho adapts Robert Bloch’s novel into a suspense story that begins with secretary Marion Crane fleeing after stealing money and checking into the isolated Bates Motel. Norman Bates, the shy proprietor, lives with his unseen mother in a looming house above it. The famous shower murder abruptly shifts the story away from Marion, while sharply edited images and Bernard Herrmann’s piercing string score make suspense central to the experience. Psycho became a landmark of mainstream horror and is especially remembered for Hitchcock’s manipulation of audience expectations: viewers are encouraged to change whom they identify with as the mystery unfolds.

key_facts.text: The film opened in 1960 and stars Janet Leigh as Marion Crane and Anthony Perkins as Norman Bates.
Psycho is based on Robert Bloch’s 1959 novel; Joseph Stefano wrote the screenplay.
The shower murder comes roughly 45 minutes into the film, an early and startling departure from the story’s initial focus on Marion.
Bernard Herrmann’s memorable score uses strings, including the piercing musical cue associated with the shower scene.
Hitchcock sought to protect the plot surprises by discouraging press screenings and having theaters prevent late arrivals from entering after the film began.
